intro: Project 001c explores how to accelerate a 1 kg probe to 0.001c (≈ 300 km/s, or 63 AU/yr). At Voyager 1's speed of nearly 17 km/s, reaching Proxima Centauri (4.24 light-years) would take about 75,000 yr; at 0.001c it takes about 4,240 yr, and reaching the 120 AU heliopause takes under two years. Because the rocket equation prevents chemical propellant alone from reaching 300 km/s, these concepts layer multiple methods: a high-energy launch and Jupiter gravity assist plunge the spacecraft close to the Sun, a deep Solar Oberth burn multiplies kinetic energy at peak orbital speed, and solar sails or rotating tethers add further speed.

eventTypes.burn: A conventional rocket engine burn away from the Sun's deep gravity well, typically burning liquid hydrogen/oxygen or solid propellant (specific impulse around 450 s) to inject the spacecraft onto an interplanetary transfer orbit or adjust its trajectory.
eventTypes.oberthBurn: Firing a rocket at closest approach (perihelion) deep inside the Sun's gravity well, where the spacecraft already travels at 200–370 km/s. Because kinetic energy scales with velocity squared, a modest delta-v there produces a much larger final escape speed.
eventTypes.tetherRelease: A momentum-exchange encounter with a fast-spinning orbital cable (rotovator) made of high-strength fiber such as Zylon or carbon nanotubes. The tether catches and flings the probe forward, adding roughly 3–5 km/s per station without burning onboard propellant.
eventTypes.solarSail: An ultra-thin, reflective membrane unfurled near perihelion so intense sunlight pushes the probe continuously outward. Measured by its lightness number beta (radiation force divided by solar gravity), the sail effectively weakens the Sun's gravitational pull during escape.
eventTypes.gravityAssist: An unpowered planetary flyby that bends the probe's path in the planet's gravity field. Passing behind a planet steals orbital momentum to boost solar-system speed (as Voyager did), while passing in front sheds angular momentum to plunge closely toward the Sun.
eventTypes.stp: Solar thermal propulsion routes liquid hydrogen propellant through a heat shield exposed to intense sunlight near perihelion (above 2,800 K). Exhausting superheated hydrogen achieves specific impulses of 1,000–1,250 s—more than double chemical rockets—maximizing the Solar Oberth boost.

scenarios.concept-a-baseline: After a high-energy launch and retrograde Jupiter flyby drop perihelion to 6 solar radii (0.0279 AU), a two-stage chemical burn adds 12 km/s at 251.5 km/s perihelion speed, yielding a 76.42 km/s Solar Oberth escape velocity grounded in near-term mission studies. To push further, this scenario appends a speculative outbound chain of 12 Zylon momentum-exchange tethers (3 km/s each), reaching 112.42 km/s (0.000375c, or 23.7 AU/yr) under far-field linear addition.
scenarios.concept-b-baseline: A self-contained hybrid sundiver that avoids external tether infrastructure. A Jupiter gravity assist directs the spacecraft to a 10 solar radii (0.0465 AU) perihelion, similar to Parker Solar Probe's thermal regime. At perihelion, a 6 km/s chemical kick stage fires and separates before the probe unfurls a 330 m² refractory solar sail (lightness number beta = 0.25). Combined Oberth thrust and continuous sunlight pressure yield 107.56 km/s (0.000359c, or 22.7 AU/yr).
scenarios.concept-c-baseline: An infrastructure-heavy architecture combining pre-deployed tethers with solar-thermal propulsion (STP). An inbound tether network and Jupiter assist place the vehicle on a 45 km/s hyperbolic plunge to 3.5 solar radii (0.0163 AU). There, a transpiration-cooled hydrogen STP heat-shield engine (Isp 1,000 s) fires for 24 km/s, reaching 136.36 km/s after the Oberth burn, before 15 speculative carbon-nanotube tethers (4 km/s each) raise final speed to 196.36 km/s (0.000655c, or 41.4 AU/yr).
scenarios.voyager-1: Launched in September 1977, Voyager 1 is the fastest spacecraft escaping the solar system today. After chemical departure from Earth, it relied on unpowered planetary gravity assists at Jupiter (March 1979) and Saturn (November 1980) to borrow orbital momentum from both gas giants. Its close pass by Saturn's moon Titan bent its path out of the ecliptic plane, leaving it cruising outward at roughly 16.9 km/s (3.6 AU/yr).
scenarios.voyager-2: Launched in August 1977, Voyager 2 flew the rare four-planet Grand Tour across the outer solar system. Successive gravity assists at Jupiter (1979), Saturn (1981), and Uranus (1986) accelerated the spacecraft and aimed it toward Neptune (1989). Diving over Neptune's north pole to observe its moon Triton bent the trajectory south of the ecliptic, leaving Voyager 2 escaping the Sun at roughly 15.2 km/s (3.2 AU/yr).
